biggestWin: Give the plot a reserved right-hand gutter and let the three right-edge labels — the axis maximum, the best-week tag and the live week's value — each own a line inside it instead of all three landing on the same 100px of the top-right corner. One change fixes the two worst findings at once: the previous-best label starts painting at all, and "12 so far" stops overprinting the axis maximum "12" at every width. That corner is where the whole question "better or worse than my normal" is answered, and right now it is the only illegible place on the surface.

findings.problem: The label "Best week · 8" is in the DOM at full opacity and never reaches the screen. `.record` is a 1px-tall box (`height: 0` plus `border-top`), and its `draw` keyframes end on `clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0)` with `animation-fill-mode: both`. That fill sits above the `[data-motion="settled"] .record { clip-path: none }` rule in the cascade, so the clip is always applied and always resolves to the 1px border box. The tag is positioned at `top: -18px`, entirely outside it, and is clipped away. Verified at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440, on both grounds, under `?motion=settled`, `?motion=play` after the 1.7s choreography, and the webdriver default: `document.elementFromPoint` at the tag's own centre returns `.colw`, never the tag. Overriding `.record { animation: none !important; clip-path: none !important }` makes "BEST WEEK · 8" appear immediately — and reveals a second problem underneath, that the tag then sits behind the hatched partial-week bar, which overprints "K ·".
findings.consequence: The owner sees a dashed rule crossing the chart at two-thirds height with nothing naming it. A dashed reference line in a chart conventionally reads as a target or a threshold, so she is invited to conclude "I am above the line" without being told what the line is or that it is worth 8. The one comparison the movement exists to make — is this stretch better than my normal — is drawn and left unlabelled. The screen-reader line does say "The best week before this one was 8", so the spoken reading carries the fact and the visual one does not: the sighted reader gets strictly less.
findings.fix: Take the tag out of the clipped box. Move `.record-tag` from a child of `.record` to a sibling absolutely positioned inside `.plot` at `bottom: calc(var(--r) * 1%)` with its own `margin-bottom: 4px`, keeping `right: 0` and the `t-label` role. Then reserve the space it needs: add `padding-right: 96px` to `.plot`'s `.cols`, `.record` and `.gridline` rules so the twelfth column no longer runs under the right-hand labels, and give `.record-tag` `background: var(--paper); padding-left: var(--gap-hair)` as it already has. If the entrance is still wanted, animate the tag's own `opacity` rather than clipping its parent.
findings.assertion: In state=full at each declared viewport, on both grounds, and under motion=settled, motion=play (sampled after 2000ms) and the webdriver default, `document.elementFromPoint` at the centre of `.record-tag` returns `.record-tag` or a descendant of it, AND no ancestor of `.record-tag` computes a `clip-path` other than `none`, AND the tag's rect intersects no `.bar`.

findings.element: .bar-val ("12 so far") against .gridline b ("12") at the top right of the plot
findings.problem: The live week's value label and the top gridline's value label overlap on screen at every declared viewport. Measured (light, settled, state=full): at 1440 `.bar-val` is 1204–1272 × 385–400 and the "12" gridline label is 1246–1265 × 392–407 — a 19 × 8px overprint; at 1280 the same; at 768 the same; at 390 `.bar-val` is 304–372 and the label 330–349. The "FAR" of "12 SO FAR" is struck through by a second numeral that happens also to read 12, so two different facts (this week's count and the axis maximum) are drawn on top of each other in the same 11px tracked mono. `.bar-val` also overhangs `.plot`'s right edge by 7px at 1280/1440, 12px at 768 and 23px at 390 — at 390 that carries it past the `.page`'s own 24px right margin. Present in full, partial, quiet and loading, on both grounds; the dark ground is worse because both labels sit on the same #18181b card.
findings.consequence: The single most important column on the chart — the week the owner is living in — has its value printed illegibly, over the number that establishes the scale. She either misreads one for the other or, more likely, reads neither and loses both the current count and the chart's magnitude. On a phone the label also breaks the page's right margin, which is the one edge every other element on the surface respects.
findings.fix: Right-align the live week's value instead of centring it over a column that is already at the plot's right edge: replace `.bar-val { left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%) }` with `.bar-val { left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%) } .colw:last-child .bar-val { left: auto; right: 0; transform: none; }`, and raise the top gridline's label clear by changing `.gridline b { top: -14px }` to `.gridline:last-of-type b { top: -30px }` for the 100% line only. Combined with the right gutter in `record-tag-never-paints`, the three right-edge labels then stack: axis max, best-week tag, this week's value.
findings.assertion: In every state that draws `.bar-val`, at each declared viewport and on both grounds, `.bar-val`'s rect intersects no `.gridline b`, no `.record-tag` and no `.xaxis span`, and `.bar-val.getBoundingClientRect().right <= .plot.getBoundingClientRect().right`.

findings.element: .kpis — the five cards over the shared denominator, movement two
findings.problem: The row is built to be read across and shares no horizontal line. Two separate breaks, measured at 1280 and 1440 (state=full, light): (a) the lead card's `9` has its `.t-num` box at top 843 / bottom 879 while the other four sit at 849 / 884 — a 6px baseline offset, because the lead card's first slot is an 11px `.t-label` (line box 14.85px) and the other four carry a 20px `.glyph`; (b) `haven't moved in a fortnight` and `past the day they were due` set on one line while `have nobody's name on them` and `are waiting on something else` wrap to two, each ending on a single orphaned word ("them", "else"), which pushes their meters from top 920 to top 940 — a 20px stagger across the row. At 390 all four wrap and the meters agree; at 768 none wrap and they agree; it breaks at exactly the two desk widths the product is designed at.
findings.consequence: The meters are the only comparable marks in the row and the row's whole claim is that all five read the same 9. Two of them sit 20px below the others, so the eye cannot sweep the bar lengths against a common line and has to re-find each one. The five figures likewise sit on two baselines, which reads as a row that was assembled rather than set. Two cards ending on a one-word line makes the row look ragged before anything is read at all.
findings.fix: Two rules. Give the top slot one height in every card: add `.kpi .glyph, .kpi.lead .t-label { height: 20px; display: grid; place-items: center; }` with `.kpi.lead .t-label { place-items: center start; }` so the numerals share a baseline. Then pin the meter to the bottom of the card: add `.kpi .meter, .kpi .na, .kpi .t-label:last-of-type { margin-top: auto; }` so the word block can wrap to one or two lines without moving it. Leave the words themselves alone.
findings.assertion: At each declared viewport and on both grounds, in state=full and state=partial, every `.kpi .t-num` shares the same `getBoundingClientRect().bottom` within 1px, and every `.kpi .meter` shares the same `getBoundingClientRect().top` within 1px.

findings.problem: The file resets `box-sizing` and nothing else, so the user-agent stylesheet's `margin: 1em 0` is live on every paragraph and heading. Measured computed margins in state=full: `.t-label` paragraphs 11px top and bottom, `.t-small` 13px, `.t-head` 20px, `.t-sect` 21.58px. The result is that the spacing between typographic blocks is set by the browser, not by the declared ladder. Inside `.limit`, a flex column with `gap: var(--gap-tight)` (8px), the rendered gap from the "Not yet" eyebrow to its heading is 39px and from the heading to its explanation 41px — the authored rung appears nowhere. Same in `.ghost-say` (headline to caption: 37px against an authored 4px), `.stack` (figure to note: 23px against 8px) and `.reading` when it wraps at 390 (49px). Because the UA margin is `1em`, the gap also scales with the font size — the exact coupling the file's own comment rejects for leading ("Leading belongs to a role, not to a size"). The audit gate cannot see this: it reads the SOURCE for raw px in margin, padding and gap, and these numbers are not in the source.
findings.consequence: Every relationship the type system expresses through proximity is wrong by three to five times. "Not yet" is meant to be an eyebrow sitting on top of "Open work over time"; at 39px away it reads as an unrelated stamp, and the refusal tiles lose the grouping that makes them scan as three of a kind. The whole surface reads looser and taller than it was drawn — the phone's refusal tiles are 216px tall to hold three short lines — so a reader scrolls further to reach less.
findings.fix: Add `h1, h2, h3, p { margin: 0; }` immediately after the `* { box-sizing: border-box; }` rule, then re-check the four places that were silently relying on the browser's gap and give them a rung from the ladder: `.limit` and `.ghost-say` move from `--gap-tight` to `--gap-snug`, `.stack` from `--gap-tight` to `--gap-line`, and `.reading` keeps `--gap-snug`.
findings.assertion: In every state, at every declared viewport, every rendered `p`, `h1`, `h2`, `h3` and `h4` computes `margin-top: 0px` and `margin-bottom: 0px`; and every non-zero computed `gap`, `margin` and `padding` on the surface is one of the declared `--gap-*` rungs.

findings.element: .coverage — the source-and-provenance strip at the foot of every state
findings.problem: The micro-label voice (11px Geist Mono, weight 400, `letter-spacing: 0.09em`, uppercase) has no upper bound on string length, and the longest string on the surface is set in it. The `.coverage` block carries 246–267 characters of `data-type="label"` depending on state, of which the lab clause alone is 134: "LAB WEEKLY COUNTS AND AGES ARE LAB-AUTHORED; HARBOUR HOUSE WEDDINGS, ORLA, THE READING DATE AND THE 9 ARE BOUND TO THE SHIPPING FIXTURE". At 390 it renders as a four-line, 133px-tall paragraph of tracked uppercase mono. Every other label on the surface is a stamp of 12–36 characters, which is what the voice is for; this one is a sentence with a semicolon and three clauses. Tracked uppercase mono destroys word shape, and word shape is what makes a sentence scannable — the two are directly opposed.
findings.consequence: The line that discloses which figures are real and which are lab-authored — the surface's own honesty statement, and the thing a sceptical owner would look for — is the hardest text on the page to read. It is set the way a legal disclaimer is set, which is exactly the reading it will get: skipped.
findings.fix: Split the strip's voice. Keep the four short source stamps (`Tasks answered`, `Timeline answered`, `Notes answered, for you`, `Read 09:14…`) in `t-label`, and move the lab clause to its own line below them in `t-small dim`: change the last `` in `shell()`'s `.coverage` block to `Lab …` and add `.coverage .t-small { text-transform: none; letter-spacing: var(--track-flat); max-width: 68ch; }`.
findings.assertion: In every state, at every declared viewport, no element carrying `data-type="label"` contains more than 48 characters of visible text, and no element carrying `data-type="label"` renders on more than two lines.

findings.element: .reading .rule — the hairline between the reading instant and the window
findings.problem: The reading line is a flex row of two label stamps with a `flex: 1 1 40px` hairline between them, so the rule's job is to join the left stamp to the right one. At 390 the row wraps: measured, the date stamp occupies 24–297 at top 192, the rule renders as a 57px stub at 309–366 pointing at nothing, and "TWELVE WEEKS" drops to a second line at top 241 with empty space to its right. The rule survives the wrap as decoration with no function.
findings.consequence: A hairline that connects nothing is the kind of stray mark a reader's eye stops on and then has to dismiss, at the top of the screen, before the reading has started. The two stamps also stop reading as one line of context and become two unrelated fragments, which is the opposite of what the reading line is for.
findings.fix: Below 560px, drop the rule and set the reading as a single line: inside the existing `@media (max-width: 560px)` block add `.reading { gap: var(--gap-tight); } .reading .rule { display: none; } .reading p:not(:last-child)::after { content: " ·"; }` so the two stamps join with the same middot the rest of the surface uses.
findings.assertion: At 390 in every state, either every child of `.reading` shares a `getBoundingClientRect().top` within 2px, or `.reading .rule` computes `display: none`.

findings.element: the quiet state's clear-all sentence, and the accessible name built in kpi()
findings.problem: Two strings concatenate a number with a verb phrase that was written for one count only. On screen in `state=quiet`: "All 9 open jobs **has** moved inside a fortnight, none is past its day, and every one has a name on it." — `plural(D.open, "open job", "open jobs")` produces a plural subject and the verb is hard-coded singular. In the accessibility tree in every state that renders the unowned card: "1 job **have** nobody's name on them, of 9 jobs open" — `kpi()` builds `${plural(n, "job", "jobs")} ${word}` where `word` is a fixed plural phrase.
findings.consequence: The quiet state is the one moment the product tells the owner nothing is wrong, and it says it in a broken sentence — the surface reads as assembled by a machine at precisely the point it is asking to be believed. The screen-reader reading of the unowned card is ungrammatical every time it is spoken, on every state, which is the one channel a reader cannot skim past.
findings.fix: In the quiet view, replace `All ${plural(D.open, "open job", "open jobs")} has moved` with `Every one of the ${plural(D.open, "open job", "open jobs")} has moved`. In `kpi()`, change the accessible-name template from `` `${plural(n, "job", "jobs")} ${word}, of …` `` to `` `${n} of ${plural(D.open, "open job", "open jobs")}: ${word}` ``, which agrees for every count including 1 and 0 without a second phrasing.
findings.assertion: For every state and both grounds, the rendered text and every accessible name are free of the patterns /\bjobs\s+(has|is|was)\b/ and /\b1 job\s+(have|are|were)\b/.

findings.element: .rail i — the four navigation glyphs at top left
findings.problem: The rail draws U+2302 ⌂, U+270E ✎, U+2611 ☑ and U+2197 ↗ with `font-family: Geist`. Geist does not carry the first three. Probed with `canvas.measureText` at 13px: ⌂ measures 7.8px under Geist, Geist Mono, serif and system-ui alike, ✎ measures 13px under all of them and ☑ 11.2px under all of them — identical widths meaning one fallback font is painting them in every case — while the control glyph "A" measures 8.68 under Geist against 9.39 serif and 8.39 system-ui, and ↗ measures 8.07 under Geist against 9.52 elsewhere, so Geist really does carry that one. Three of the four rail marks are therefore drawn by whatever the OS supplies. The audit's family check cannot see it: it reads computed `font-family`, which reports what the author wrote ("Geist"), not what the compositor painted.
findings.consequence: The first four objects at the top left of every frame at 768 and above are the only shapes on the surface not drawn by a face the studio chose, and they change between Windows, macOS and Linux — so the same screenshot is not the same product. On systems that resolve U+2611 to an emoji face it would also paint in colour, outside the eighteen.
findings.fix: Replace the four glyph characters in `shell()`'s `.rail` markup with inline SVG paths at 13px in `currentColor`, drawn on the same 12×12 grid as the four status marks in `ICON`, so the rail is vector like the rest of the surface and no text is set in a face outside the two.
findings.assertion: For every character rendered on the surface, the glyph is covered by Geist or Geist Mono — measured by comparing `canvas.measureText(ch)` under `13px Geist` and `13px "Geist Mono"` against `13px serif` and `13px monospace` and requiring at least one declared family to differ from every control family, not by reading computed `font-family`.
